items.q: Why do planets stay in orbit around the Sun?
items.correct: Gravity provides a centripetal force pulling them into a curved path.
items.misconception: There is no force on an orbiting planet.
items.random_wrong: The solar wind pushes them around.
items.why: Without a centripetal force a planet would move off in a straight line; gravity constantly changes its direction.

items.q: What does red-shift of distant galaxies show?
items.correct: They are moving away — the universe is expanding.
items.why: Stretched (red-shifted) light from receding galaxies is key evidence for an expanding universe.

items.correct: A distance — how far light travels in a year.
items.random_wrong: The time light takes to reach Earth from the Sun.
items.why: Despite the name, a light-year measures distance (~9.5×10¹⁵ m).

items.q: What causes the phases of the Moon?
items.correct: We see different amounts of the sunlit half as the Moon orbits Earth.
items.misconception: Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
items.random_wrong: The Moon producing its own light.
items.why: Phases come from the changing angle of the sunlit Moon; Earth's shadow causes eclipses, not phases.

items.correct: The tilt of Earth's axis, changing the angle and hours of sunlight.
items.misconception: Earth being closer to the Sun in summer.
items.random_wrong: The Sun getting hotter in summer.
items.why: Axial tilt, not distance, drives the seasons; Earth's distance from the Sun barely changes.

items.q: What happens to a star like the Sun at the end of its life?
items.correct: It becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf.
items.misconception: It explodes as a supernova and forms a black hole.
items.why: Only massive stars end as supernovae/black holes; low-mass stars become red giants then white dwarfs.
